summary: We developed an interactive, web-based Planetary Analog Mission Control platform that integrates NASA open data in order to identify, compare, contrast, and simulate high-fidelity terrestrial analogs for future Moon and Mars bases. This is important due to the fact that missions in these places are expensive and strategies to optimize these costs need to be taken. Specifically, our tool pairs Cotahuasi Canyon (Peru) with Jezero Crater (Mars) for fluvio-volcanic stratigraphy and rover mobility, and Lanzarote (Canary Islands) with Marius Hills (Moon) for volcanic domes, and subterranean habitat potential. To address the challenge, the platform evaluates a weighted Analog Similarity Index that includes topography, mineralogy, and environmental profiles, at the same time is paired with orbital maps and a dual-surface Rocker-Bogie physics simulator that models traction, wheel slip, and obstacles under Earth, Martian, and Lunar gravities.
details:
Space in Our Planet is an interactive web platform designed to identify, validate, and simulate overlooked terrestrial locations where space agencies can test rovers, sensors, and habitat concepts before deploying to the Moon and Mars.Because no single environment on Earth replicates every extraterrestrial condition simultaneously, our team first analyzed planetary orbital data to establish baseline environmental and geological thresholds, including reduced gravity, relief, slope angles (>10 degrees), boulder granulometry (D50D50​), mineralogy, and thermal ranges.

Using official NASA open datasets, such as: ASTER GDEM, SRTM, among others; we matched these planetary benchmarks to two high-value terrestrial analogs: Cotahuasi Canyon (Peru) as a fluvio-volcanic analog for Jezero Crater, and Lanzarote (Canary Islands) as a basaltic lava-tube and volcanic-dome analog for Marius Hills. To translate these comparisons into actionable engineering insights, we developed a custom Mission Control web application using HTML5, Java Script, and incorporating Synthetic Intelligence (SI)-assisted coding workflows to build an interactive Rocker-Bogie physics and wheel-slip simulator.

Through this unified interface, users can explore synchronized orbital maps, evaluate a weighted Analog Similarity Index, and test rover traction and obstacle navigation side-by-side under Earth, Martian, and Lunar gravities across real terrain substrates. By combining open NASA geospatial data with accessible browser-based physics simulations, our project reduces mission risk and lowers the barrier for engineers, researchers, and students to validate rover autonomy,regolith mechanics, and radiation-shielded subterranean habitats right here on Earth.
